key_insight: ASR auditing should be stakeholder-driven: involving affected communities and domain experts produces more meaningful, contextualized evaluations than relying on narrow technical metrics alone.
problem_solved: Addresses the gap where automatic speech recognition (ASR) evaluation focuses on aggregate metrics (e.g., WER) and overlooks harms to underrepresented speakers, accessibility needs, and real-world deployment contexts due to lack of stakeholder involvement.
method: Stakeholder mapping and participatory design: engage end users, linguists, accessibility advocates, clinicians, and domain experts to define harms, priorities, and evaluation criteria.
Multi-dimensional audits: pair quantitative tests (demographic-disaggregated error rates, robustness to accents/noise) with qualitative methods (user studies, contextual impact assessments).
Transparent reporting and iterative remediation: publish audit findings, establish governance processes, and use stakeholder feedback loops to guide model fixes and deployment decisions.
impact: Promotes more robust, equitable, and accountable ASR systems by revealing contextual harms early and guiding targeted mitigation; helps practitioners meet ethical, legal, and user-centered requirements in real-world deployments.
visual_elements: Stakeholder map diagram showing groups (e.g., speakers with diverse accents, disability communities, clinicians, regulators) and their roles in the audit.
Audit workflow timeline: co-design → quantitative tests → qualitative assessments → remediation → re-audit.
Comparison chart: aggregate metric (WER) vs demographic-disaggregated error rates to illustrate hidden disparities.
Icon set representing types of evaluation (data, users, metrics, governance) for quick visual summary.
paper_title: The case for stakeholder-driven AI auditing in automatic speech recognition
paper_authors: Mona Sloane, Hilke Schellmann, Katelyn Xiaoying Mei, Anna Seo Gyeong Choi, Allison Koenecke
